title: Richard II
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. A Room in the palace
openingText: King Richard sits in judgment as two great lords, Bolingbroke and Mowbray, accuse each other of treason and demand the right to settle it in single combat.
about:
Richard II tells how an anointed king lost his crown. Richard is eloquent, vain and extravagant. When his cousin Henry Bolingbroke and the Duke of Norfolk accuse each other of treason, Richard stops their trial by combat at the last moment and banishes them both. When Bolingbroke's father, John of Gaunt, dies, Richard seizes his lands to pay for a war in Ireland.

While Richard is away, Bolingbroke returns to claim his inheritance. The nobles flock to him, Richard's support melts away, and the king is forced to give up the crown in a famous scene of public humiliation. Imprisoned at Pomfret Castle, Richard reflects on what is left of a king once the crown is gone, before he is murdered.

Written entirely in verse around 1595, the play is the first in Shakespeare's series about the Wars of the Roses, continued in Henry IV and Henry V. It contains Gaunt's speech on 'this England' and some of Shakespeare's most beautiful poetry about kingship and loss.

whyItMatters.title: What makes a ruler legitimate
whyItMatters.body: Richard has the right to rule but rules badly; Bolingbroke rules well but has no right. The play refuses to make the choice easy, and the question returns in every argument about power.

whyItMatters.title: A king who becomes a person
whyItMatters.body: Richard is hardest to like when he has power and most human when he loses it. His prison speeches turn a political story into one about identity.

whyItMatters.title: Poetry as character
whyItMatters.body: Every character speaks verse, but Richard turns his own fall into poetry. Readers can watch how language can be both a weakness and a kind of strength.

angleCards.title: Richard against Bolingbroke
angleCards.text: Track who has right, who has power, and how the balance shifts scene by scene.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare Richard and Bolingbroke and decide which of them the play supports.

angleCards.title: The language of kingship
angleCards.text: Notice the images of the sun, the crown and the mirror, and what Richard does with them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the play's images of kingship and see how Richard's language changes as he loses power.

angleCards.title: England as a garden
angleCards.text: Read Gaunt's speech and the gardeners' scene closely. What does the play think a country is?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the play's ideas about England and good government through its garden imagery.

angleCards.title: Loyalty
angleCards.text: Watch York, Aumerle and Northumberland. Who stays loyal, to whom, and at what cost?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how each noble chooses between loyalty to the king and loyalty to the country.

cast.name: King Richard II
cast.description: Proud, poetic and reckless with money, he believes God protects his crown. He loses it to his cousin and finds himself only in defeat.

cast.name: Henry Bolingbroke
cast.description: Richard's cousin, banished and then disinherited. He returns to reclaim his lands and ends as King Henry IV.

cast.name: John of Gaunt
cast.description: Duke of Lancaster, Bolingbroke's father and Richard's uncle. On his deathbed he warns Richard and praises England.

cast.name: The Duke of York
cast.description: Another of Richard's uncles, left in charge of England, torn between loyalty to the king and the need to accept the new order.

cast.name: The Queen
cast.description: She senses disaster before it comes and says a painful farewell to Richard on his way to prison.

cast.name: Aumerle
cast.description: Richard's loyal friend, whose part in a plot against the new king puts his own family in conflict.
